title: Incident Zero
blurb: Four sequences behind a breach: the response model, the DR activation, the evidence-handling order, and the attacker's own path through the kill chain.
source: Chapple CISSP SG 10ed ch.17 (Preventing and Responding to Incidents) · ch.18 (Disaster Recovery Planning) · ch.19 (Investigations and Ethics) · outline 7.6/7.11/7.1 · MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise Matrix, as published at attack.mitre.org

ladders.title: Bracknell Freight: the response
ladders.prompt: A SOC analyst at Bracknell Freight confirms a server compromise. Order the incident response from first detection to closing the loop.

steps.label: Detection
steps.detail: A SIEM alert or an end-user report surfaces something abnormal; the analyst's job here is to triage and confirm this is an actual incident, not just a benign event, before anything else moves (SG).

steps.label: Response
steps.detail: Once confirmed, the IR team is activated: it verifies what is affected, sizes up the damage and starts protecting evidence so the next step can act on facts; jumping straight to root-cause analysis or a press notice at this point is the tested trap, not the correct next move (SG).

steps.label: Mitigation
steps.detail: With the scope known, the team contains it, for example by isolating the compromised server from the network and disabling the accounts in use; the job at this stage is not yet to fix the underlying problem, only to limit the scope and stop it from getting worse (SG).

steps.label: Reporting
steps.detail: Once the incident is contained, formal reporting goes out to stakeholders — and to regulators or affected individuals where law or contract (such as a payment-card standard) requires it; reporting is not the first move, it follows containment, not detection (SG).

steps.label: Recovery
steps.detail: Systems are restored to a fully functioning state — rebuilding from clean images and known-good backups is the most defensible path, not simply patching in place (SG).

steps.label: Remediation
steps.detail: A root-cause analysis identifies what allowed the incident to happen, and configuration changes are made so it cannot recur the same way — this is a distinct step from recovery, which only restores service (SG).

steps.label: Lessons Learned
steps.detail: The IR team and stakeholders review the whole response, and findings feed back into detection tuning and future preparation — this closes the loop rather than ending the process at remediation (SG).

ladders.title: Meridian Bank: activating the DR plan
ladders.prompt: Meridian Bank's primary data center goes dark. Order the steps for activating and executing the disaster recovery plan.

steps.label: Declare the disaster against defined criteria
steps.detail: The DR plan names the person authorized to call it and the specific thresholds that must be met — this has to happen first, before any team mobilizes or any site activates, or the org risks activating for a non-event (SG).

steps.label: Notify and assemble the DR team
steps.detail: The notification checklist reaches DR team members and critical personnel through their listed contact methods, so the people who execute the plan are actually in motion (SG).

steps.label: Assess and triage the damage
steps.detail: On arrival, the team's first priority is a quick assessment of what's actually broken, followed by more detailed evaluation — skipping straight to restoration without triage risks recovering the wrong systems first (SG).

steps.label: Activate the alternate processing site
steps.detail: Based on the assessment, operations shift to the pre-arranged alternate site — a subscription hot site with near-real-time data, a partially equipped warm site, or a bare cold site, chosen well before the disaster, not decided on the fly (SG).

steps.label: Restore systems and data
steps.detail: The most critical business units get their systems back first, restoring the affected files and services that were active at the time of the failure — restoring the facility is a separate concern from recovering business operations (SG).

steps.label: Lessons learned
steps.detail: A lessons-learned session, held while memories are fresh, captures what worked, what didn't, and what the plan should change — the DR effort isn't complete until this session happens, not once systems are simply back online (SG).

ladders.title: Corvid Labs: seizing the evidence
ladders.prompt: Investigators respond to a compromised workstation at Corvid Labs. Order the evidence collection from most volatile to least volatile.
ladders.citation: outline 7.1 (evidence collection) · volatility order per RFC 3227-style practice

steps.label: CPU registers and cache
steps.detail: The most fleeting state on the machine — gone the instant execution continues or power is cut — so it has to be captured before any other step touches the system.

steps.label: RAM and running-process memory
steps.detail: Live memory holds decrypted data, injected code, and network sessions that disappear on shutdown; a memory capture must happen while the system is still running, which is why investigators are trained never to power a live system off first (SG).

steps.label: Network state (ARP cache, routing table, active connections)
steps.detail: Connection tables and cached network state decay quickly as new traffic arrives, but they persist a little longer than raw process memory, so they're pulled next.

steps.label: Temporary files and swap
steps.detail: Temp and swap data survive a reboot less reliably than disk data proper but longer than in-memory state — this sits between the volatile and the durable evidence.

steps.label: Local disk contents
steps.detail: The disk itself is comparatively durable, but a forensic acquisition still comes before archived or off-box copies — investigators create bit-for-bit images here rather than working from the original (SG).

steps.label: Remote logs, backups, and archival media
steps.detail: Centralized log servers, backup tapes, and offline archives are the least volatile — they'll still be there tomorrow, which is exactly why they're collected last, not because they matter least to the case.

ladders.title: Northgate Retail: reconstructing the intrusion
ladders.prompt: Analysts reconstruct how an attacker moved through Northgate Retail's network. Order the intrusion by ATT&CK tactic, from initial access to exfiltration.
ladders.citation: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise Matrix, as published at attack.mitre.org

steps.label: Initial Access (TA0001)
steps.detail: The attacker gets into Northgate's network — in this case a spear-phished vendor-invoice attachment opened by an accounts-payable clerk — the entry point that starts everything downstream (MITRE ATT&CK).

steps.label: Execution (TA0002)
steps.detail: The attachment's macro runs malicious code on the clerk's workstation; this is the attacker running code they control, distinct from merely having gotten a foot in the door (MITRE ATT&CK).

steps.label: Persistence (TA0003)
steps.detail: The attacker plants a scheduled task that re-launches their access after reboot — maintaining the foothold before doing anything riskier, so a routine restart doesn't cost them their access (MITRE ATT&CK).

steps.label: Privilege Escalation (TA0004)
steps.detail: From the clerk's limited account, the attacker exploits a local flaw to gain admin rights on the workstation — higher-level permissions than the compromised user started with, which is a distinct tactic from simply staying resident (MITRE ATT&CK).

steps.label: Credential Access (TA0006)
steps.detail: With admin rights, the attacker dumps cached domain credentials from the workstation — stealing account names and passwords is a separate goal from the privilege escalation that enabled it (MITRE ATT&CK).

steps.label: Lateral Movement (TA0008)
steps.detail: Using the stolen credentials, the attacker moves from the clerk's workstation to the inventory database server — moving through the environment, not merely discovering it (MITRE ATT&CK).

steps.label: Exfiltration (TA0010)
steps.detail: Customer payment records are staged and pushed out over an encrypted channel to attacker-controlled infrastructure — the theft of data is the last step in this reconstruction, coming only after access, footholds, and movement are all in place (MITRE ATT&CK).
